VIDEO.title: The Hidden Source of Faith | Romans 1:17
VIDEO.series: The Book of Romans, Every Word (playlist of 28 videos)

kicker: Study aid · Romans 1:16-17 · Episode 2 (#2 of 28 in the playlist)
hand: Out of God's faithfulness, into our faith
SUMMARY: The teacher spends a whole episode on two verses, Romans 1:16-17, because they state the theme of the whole letter: Paul is not ashamed of the gospel, for it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes, to the Jew first and also to the Greek. In it the righteousness of God is revealed from faith to faith, as Habakkuk wrote, 'But the righteous will live by faith.' Paul will circle back to this thread again and again.

Why say 'I am not ashamed' when nothing in 1:1-15 hints at shame? Paul's letters answer real situations, so perhaps believers in Rome were ashamed of the gospel's simplicity or apparent foolishness. Compare 1 Corinthians 1:18-25: the word of the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing, but the power of God to those being saved. The teacher adds that we should not push this inference too far.

The gospel is not merely words; it is God's saving power at work. Quoting Robert Mounce, it is 'not a lifeless message, but a vibrant encounter for everyone who responds in faith.' There is an order: to the Jew first, because God chose to speak and work through Israel before the Gentiles.

The righteousness of God is tied to His salvation. In the Old Testament the two words stand in parallel: Psalm 40:10; Isaiah 46:13; 51:5-8; 61:10. The Hebrew tsedaqah means acting rightly or vindicating the one in the right; used of God and His covenant people, it means God acting rightly toward them, that is, saving them.

'From faith to faith' is disputed. The teacher's view, held with humility: out of God's faithfulness into man's faith. God's faithfulness runs through the Old Testament (Deuteronomy 32:4; Psalm 33:4), and the Septuagint of Habakkuk 2:4 reads 'the righteous one will live by my faith,' that is, by God's faithfulness.

The lesson: the gospel is not an idea but God's saving action in relationship, His covenant faithfulness extended to all who believe in Jesus Christ and respond with lives marked by faithfulness to Him. It is the invitation to know God (John 17:3), and we never outgrow it.
QUOTES: The gospel is not an idea, but God's saving action in relationship. It's his covenant faithfulness extended to all who believe in Jesus Christ and respond with lives marked by faithfulness to him.
It's not a philosophy. The gospel is power. It's not a theoretical axiom. It's active and moving through hearts and minds.
In the gospel, the righteousness of God is revealed out of God's faithfulness to man's faith.
We never outgrow the gospel. We simply grow more and more into the gospel.

method.h: Let the parallel lines teach you
method.p: Hebrew poetry often says one thing twice in parallel lines. When 'righteousness' and 'salvation' trade places line after line, the poet is telling you they belong together. Paul reads with that ear.

LSB_QUOTES.text: For I am not ashamed of the gospel, for it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes, to the Jew first and also to the Greek.
For in it the righteousness of God is revealed from faith to faith; as it is written, “But the righteous will live by faith.”
For the word of Yahweh is upright, / And all His work is done in faithfulness.

left.text: For I am not ashamed of the gospel, for it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes, to the Jew first and also to the Greek.

right.text: For the word of the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing, but to us who are being saved, it is the power of God.

lines.text: Nothing in 1:1-15 suggests Paul is embarrassed. So why deny it? Paul's letters respond to real problems: marriage questions in Corinth, life in the flesh in Galatia. If he raises shame in Rome, perhaps believers there were ashamed of the gospel's simplicity or apparent foolishness.

1 Corinthians 1 shows the same tension: 'Has not God made foolish the wisdom of the world?' (1 Corinthians 1:20), and 'the foolishness of God is wiser than men' (1 Corinthians 1:25). The teacher cautions that without Paul stating his reason, this remains an inference.

left.text: For this reason I also suffer these things, but I am not ashamed; for I know whom I have believed and I am convinced that He is able to guard what I have entrusted to Him until that day.

right.text: For whoever is ashamed of Me and My words in this adulterous and sinful generation, the Son of Man will also be ashamed of him when He comes in the glory of His Father with the holy angels.”

lines.text: Study note (added): Paul uses the same language from prison, urging Timothy, 'do not be ashamed of either the witness about our Lord or me His prisoner' (2 Timothy 1:8). Jesus Himself warned about being ashamed of Him and His words.

src.text: For I am not ashamed of the gospel, for it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes, to the Jew first and also to the Greek.

lines.text: The gospel is not a conversation or a string of words. It is God's saving power at work in people's lives: in Robert Mounce's words, quoted in the video, 'not a lifeless message, but a vibrant encounter for everyone who responds in faith.'
'To the Jew first and also to the Greek': God chose to work, move and speak through Israel first, then the Gentiles. Paul practiced this order on his journeys (Acts 13:46).

left.text: I do not conceal Your righteousness within my heart; / I speak of Your faithfulness and Your salvation; / I do not hide Your lovingkindness and Your truth from the great assembly.

right.text: “I bring near My righteousness, it is not far off; / And My salvation will not delay. / And I will grant salvation in Zion, / And My glory for Israel.

lines.text: In Hebrew poetry, terms set in parallel are treated as near-synonyms. Righteousness, faithfulness and salvation stand side by side in Psalm 40:10.

Tsedaqah: in the legal sense, acting rightly or vindicating the one in the right. In the covenant sense, God acting rightly toward His covenant people, which means saving them. The teacher shows how he found this with an interlinear and Strong's dictionary in Logos.

left.text: For the moth will eat them like a garment, / And the grub will eat them like wool. / But My righteousness will be forever, / And My salvation to all generations.”

right.text: I will rejoice greatly in Yahweh; / My soul will rejoice in my God, / For He has clothed me with garments of salvation, / He has wrapped me with a robe of righteousness, / As a bridegroom decks himself with a headdress, / And as a bride adorns herself with her jewels.

lines.text: 'My righteousness is near, My salvation has gone forth' (Isaiah 51:5); 'My salvation will be forever, And My righteousness will not be dismayed' (Isaiah 51:6). The pairing keeps returning.
Study note (added): 'He has revealed His righteousness in the eyes of the nations' (Psalm 98:2) uses the same verb idea Paul uses, 'is revealed,' with the nations in view.

left.text: for with the heart a person believes, leading to righteousness, and with the mouth he confesses, leading to salvation.

right.text: But now apart from the Law the righteousness of God has been manifested, being witnessed by the Law and the Prophets,

lines.text: Study note (added): later in the letter Paul again sets righteousness beside salvation (10:9-10) and says the righteousness of God is 'witnessed by the Law and the Prophets' (3:21), which is exactly the kind of Old Testament witness the teacher traces.

left.text: The Rock! His work is perfect, / For all His ways are just; / A God of faithfulness and without injustice, / Righteous and upright is He.

right.text: For the word of Yahweh is upright, / And all His work is done in faithfulness.

lines.text: The teacher reads 'from faith to faith' (more literally 'out of faith into faith') as out of God's faithfulness into man's faith. He argues the first 'faith' is linked to the righteousness of God, so it is God's own faithfulness to His people, the 'everyone who believes' of verse 16.
This faithfulness is God keeping His covenant promises, a theme all through the Old Testament.

FAITH.title: The righteous will live by faith

left.text: “Behold, as for the proud one, / His soul is not right within him; / But the righteous will live by his faith.

right.text: For in it the righteousness of God is revealed from faith to faith; as it is written, “But the righteous will live by faith.”

lines.text: The Hebrew reads 'by his faith.' The Septuagint, the Greek translation Paul knew well, reads as the Lord speaking: 'the righteous one will live by my faith.' Paul quotes the line without either pronoun.

If the teacher is right, Romans says again and again that the righteousness of God is revealed out of God's faithfulness to man's faithful response. He says plainly that he could be wrong, and that Christians are undecided on the phrase.
Study note (added): Habakkuk 2:4 is quoted twice more in the New Testament: Galatians 3:11 and Hebrews 10:38, where the LSB reads 'But My righteous one shall live by faith.'

left.text: And this is eternal life, that they may know You, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom You have sent.

right.text: But you are a chosen family, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for God’s own possession, so that you may proclaim the excellencies of Him who has called you out of darkness into His marvelous light;

lines.text: A propositional statement, even a true one, has no power to make dead souls alive. The gospel does, because it is God's invitation to know Him, to join His feast and be clothed in robes of righteousness, the cost of entry paid by the blood of Christ.
The teacher's mentor told him, 'We never outgrow the gospel. We simply grow more and more into the gospel,' and 'It's the gospel that saves and it's the gospel that sanctifies.'

TERMS.def: The good news; here, 'the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes' (Romans 1:16).
God's active strength; the video stresses the gospel as an encounter, not a lifeless message.
God acting rightly, especially in saving His covenant people; paired with salvation in the Psalms and Isaiah.
Literally 'out of faith into faith.' The video reads it as out of God's faithfulness into human faith; other readings exist (see Debates).
The Greek translation of the Hebrew Scriptures; its Habakkuk 2:4 reads 'by my faith.'
Hebrew poetry's habit of restating a line in different words; it shows which words belong together.

BACKGROUND.p: Ancient speeches and letters often stated the main claim early. Most commentators treat Romans 1:16-17 as the letter's theme, unpacked from 1:18 onward.
Rome prized honor; a crucified Lord looked shameful to Greeks and Romans and a stumbling block to many Jews (1 Corinthians 1:23). Saying 'I am not ashamed' answers that pressure.
Habakkuk complained that God would use the Babylonians to judge Judah (Habakkuk 1:6). God's answer (2:2-4) calls for steady trust while the vision waits for its time.
Paul often quotes the Septuagint. In Habakkuk 2:4 the Hebrew has 'his faith' and the main Septuagint text 'my faith'; Paul's quotation has neither.

DEBATES.p: Readings include: faith from first to last (faith all the way through); growing faith; the faith of the preacher to the faith of the hearer; Old Testament faith to New Testament faith; and the video's reading, God's faithfulness to human faith. The Greek allows several; context decides.

The teacher infers that some in Rome were ashamed of the gospel. Others read 'not ashamed' as a figure of speech for 'proud of,' with no problem in Rome implied. Chrysostom (Witnesses) took the teacher's line: Paul is teaching them not to be ashamed.
A quality God has, a status God gives, or God's saving action? The video stresses saving action, rooted in the Old Testament. Many hold that Paul's phrase includes more than one of these.

CAREFUL_INTRO: Small slips worth knowing (offered gently; the video's main points stand):
CAREFUL: The video reads Psalm 40:10 as 'I have not hidden your deliverance within my heart'; the LSB reads 'I do not conceal Your righteousness within my heart.' The Hebrew word is tsedaqah, which is the video's point.
Romans 1:17 in the LSB reads 'from faith to faith'; the video's translation reads 'from faith for faith.'
The video says the Septuagint of Habakkuk 2:4 reads 'my faith.' That is the main Septuagint text; some manuscripts place 'my' with 'righteous one,' as Hebrews 10:38 does ('My righteous one').
The captions spell the commentator 'Robert Mounts' and the Greek 'eistos'; read as Robert Mounce and ek pisteōs ('out of faith').

QUESTIONS: Have you ever felt embarrassed by the gospel's simplicity? What helps you not to be ashamed?
How does seeing 'righteousness' and 'salvation' as parallel change how you hear 'the righteousness of God'?
Which reading of 'from faith to faith' do you find most convincing, and why?
What is the difference between treating the gospel as a proposition and receiving it as God's power?
In what ways are you still 'growing into' the gospel?
APPLICATION_VIDEO: The gospel is not an idea, but God's saving action in relationship: His covenant faithfulness extended to all who believe in Jesus Christ and respond with lives marked by faithfulness to Him. The teacher confesses that as a young believer he treated the gospel as a proposition to defend with arguments. A mentor's words changed that: 'We never outgrow the gospel. We simply grow more and more into the gospel.' God was under no obligation to choose any of us (1 Peter 2:9); what we deserved was wrath, and what He gave was the power of His salvation.
APPLICATION_ADDED: Study note (added): this week, read Romans 1:16-17 each morning and name one place where you are tempted to be quiet about Jesus; ask God for courage there.

The teacher adds that we should not push this inference too far.

   Isaiah (Isaiah 61:10, LSB): "I will rejoice greatly in Yahweh; / My soul will rejoice in my God, / For He has clothed me with garments of salvation, / He has wrapped me with a robe of righteousness, / As a bridegroom decks himself with a headdress, / And as a bride adorns herself with her jewels."
   (video) 'My righteousness is near, My salvation has gone forth' (Isaiah 51:5); 'My salvation will be forever, And My righteousness will not be dismayed' (Isaiah 51:6). The pairing keeps returning. (Isaiah 51:5; Isaiah 51:6)
   [Background] Study note (added): 'He has revealed His righteousness in the eyes of the nations' (Psalm 98:2) uses the same verb idea Paul uses, 'is revealed,' with the nations in view. (Psalm 98:2)
3. Romans 10:9-10; 3:21-22: Paul keeps the pair together
   Paul (Romans 10:10, LSB): "for with the heart a person believes, leading to righteousness, and with the mouth he confesses, leading to salvation."
   Paul (Romans 3:21, LSB): "But now apart from the Law the righteousness of God has been manifested, being witnessed by the Law and the Prophets,"
   [Background] Study note (added): later in the letter Paul again sets righteousness beside salvation (10:9-10) and says the righteousness of God is 'witnessed by the Law and the Prophets' (3:21), which is exactly the kind of Old Testament witness the teacher traces. (Romans 10:9-10; Romans 3:21-22)

## From faith to faith
1. Deuteronomy 32:4; Psalm 33:4: A God of faithfulness
   Moses (Deuteronomy 32:4, LSB): "The Rock! His work is perfect, / For all His ways are just; / A God of faithfulness and without injustice, / Righteous and upright is He."
   Psalmist (Psalm 33:4, LSB): "For the word of Yahweh is upright, / And all His work is done in faithfulness."
   (video) The teacher reads 'from faith to faith' (more literally 'out of faith into faith') as out of God's faithfulness into man's faith. He argues the first 'faith' is linked to the righteousness of God, so it is God's own faithfulness to His people, the 'everyone who believes' of verse 16.
   (video) This faithfulness is God keeping His covenant promises, a theme all through the Old Testament.
2. Habakkuk 2:4; Romans 1:17: The righteous will live by faith
   Habakkuk (Habakkuk 2:4, LSB): "“Behold, as for the proud one, / His soul is not right within him; / But the righteous will live by his faith."
   Paul (Romans 1:17, LSB): "For in it the righteousness of God is revealed from faith to faith; as it is written, “But the righteous will live by faith.”"
   (video) The Hebrew reads 'by his faith.' The Septuagint, the Greek translation Paul knew well, reads as the Lord speaking: 'the righteous one will live by my faith.' Paul quotes the line without either pronoun.
   (video) If the teacher is right, Romans says again and again that the righteousness of God is revealed out of God's faithfulness to man's faithful response. He says plainly that he could be wrong, and that Christians are undecided on the phrase.
   [Background] Study note (added): Habakkuk 2:4 is quoted twice more in the New Testament: Galatians 3:11 and Hebrews 10:38, where the LSB reads 'But My righteous one shall live by faith.' (Galatians 3:11; Hebrews 10:38)
3. John 17:3; 1 Peter 2:9: The gospel is an invitation
   Jesus (John 17:3, LSB): "And this is eternal life, that they may know You, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom You have sent."
   Peter (1 Peter 2:9, LSB): "But you are a chosen family, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for God’s own possession, so that you may proclaim the excellencies of Him who has called you out of darkness into His marvelous light;"
   (video) A propositional statement, even a true one, has no power to make dead souls alive. The gospel does, because it is God's invitation to know Him, to join His feast and be clothed in robes of righteousness, the cost of entry paid by the blood of Christ.
   (video) The teacher's mentor told him, 'We never outgrow the gospel. We simply grow more and more into the gospel,' and 'It's the gospel that saves and it's the gospel that sanctifies.'

## Key people
- Paul: Not ashamed of the gospel; states the theme of his letter. [Background] He writes to a church he has not yet visited, so he lays out the heart of his message first.
- Habakkuk: Quoted by Paul: the righteous will live by faith. [Background] A prophet of Judah who wrestled with God over the coming Babylonian invasion; 2:4 is God's answer to him.
- David: Psalm 40:10 pairs righteousness and salvation. [Background] Psalm 40's heading calls it a Psalm of David.
- Isaiah: Four passages where righteousness and salvation stand in parallel. [Background] Isaiah 40-66 speaks often of God's righteousness as His saving action for His people.
- Robert Mounce: Quoted: the gospel is 'not a lifeless message, but a vibrant encounter.' [Background] The captions read 'Robert Mounts'; Robert H. Mounce wrote a Romans commentary (New American Commentary). The video gives no title, so check the quote before citing it.
- Jews and Greeks: The gospel goes to the Jew first and also to the Greek. [Background] 'Greek' here stands for the non-Jewish world; Paul uses the same order for judgment and glory (2:9-10).

## Places [Background]
- Rome (named in the video): The church Paul writes to; perhaps ashamed of the gospel.
- Corinth (named in the video): Where Paul writes; 1 Corinthians 1 speaks of the cross as foolishness.
- Jerusalem: To the Jew first: the gospel began here.
- Pisidian Antioch: 'It was necessary that the word of God be spoken to you first' (Acts 13:46).

## Key terms
- Gospel: The good news; here, 'the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes' (Romans 1:16).
- Power of God: God's active strength; the video stresses the gospel as an encounter, not a lifeless message.
- Righteousness of God: God acting rightly, especially in saving His covenant people; paired with salvation in the Psalms and Isaiah.
- From faith to faith: Literally 'out of faith into faith.' The video reads it as out of God's faithfulness into human faith; other readings exist (see Debates).
- Septuagint (LXX): The Greek translation of the Hebrew Scriptures; its Habakkuk 2:4 reads 'by my faith.'
- Parallelism: Hebrew poetry's habit of restating a line in different words; it shows which words belong together. [Background]

## Historical and cultural background [Background: established]
- A thesis statement: Ancient speeches and letters often stated the main claim early. Most commentators treat Romans 1:16-17 as the letter's theme, unpacked from 1:18 onward.
- Shame and honor: Rome prized honor; a crucified Lord looked shameful to Greeks and Romans and a stumbling block to many Jews (1 Corinthians 1:23). Saying 'I am not ashamed' answers that pressure.
- Habakkuk's setting: Habakkuk complained that God would use the Babylonians to judge Judah (Habakkuk 1:6). God's answer (2:2-4) calls for steady trust while the vision waits for its time.
- Which Bible did Paul quote?: Paul often quotes the Septuagint. In Habakkuk 2:4 the Hebrew has 'his faith' and the main Septuagint text 'my faith'; Paul's quotation has neither.

## Early witnesses [Background: sourced]
- John Chrysostom (c. AD 391): "I am not ashamed, having still to teach them not to be ashamed." Homilies on Romans 2, on 1:16. NPNF 1.11 (public domain).
- John Chrysostom (c. AD 391): "For you do not achieve it by toilings and labors, but you receive it by a gift from above, contributing one thing only from your own store, believing." Homilies on Romans 2, on 1:17. NPNF 1.11 (public domain).
- John Chrysostom (c. AD 391): "For after having said, from faith to faith, he sends the hearer back to the dispensations of God, which took place thus in the Old Testament." Homilies on Romans 2, on 1:17. NPNF 1.11 (public domain).

## Where scholars differ [Background: debated]
- 'From faith to faith' (1:17) Readings include: faith from first to last (faith all the way through); growing faith; the faith of the preacher to the faith of the hearer; Old Testament faith to New Testament faith; and the video's reading, God's faithfulness to human faith. The Greek allows several; context decides.
- Who is ashamed (1:16)? The teacher infers that some in Rome were ashamed of the gospel. Others read 'not ashamed' as a figure of speech for 'proud of,' with no problem in Rome implied. Chrysostom (Witnesses) took the teacher's line: Paul is teaching them not to be ashamed.
- 'Righteousness of God' A quality God has, a status God gives, or God's saving action? The video stresses saving action, rooted in the Old Testament. Many hold that Paul's phrase includes more than one of these.

## Careful reading notes
Small slips worth knowing (offered gently; the video's main points stand):
- The video reads Psalm 40:10 as 'I have not hidden your deliverance within my heart'; the LSB reads 'I do not conceal Your righteousness within my heart.' The Hebrew word is tsedaqah, which is the video's point.
- Romans 1:17 in the LSB reads 'from faith to faith'; the video's translation reads 'from faith for faith.'
- The video says the Septuagint of Habakkuk 2:4 reads 'my faith.' That is the main Septuagint text; some manuscripts place 'my' with 'righteous one,' as Hebrews 10:38 does ('My righteous one').
- The captions spell the commentator 'Robert Mounts' and the Greek 'eistos'; read as Robert Mounce and ek pisteōs ('out of faith').

## Reflection and discussion questions
1. Have you ever felt embarrassed by the gospel's simplicity? What helps you not to be ashamed?
2. How does seeing 'righteousness' and 'salvation' as parallel change how you hear 'the righteousness of God'?
3. Which reading of 'from faith to faith' do you find most convincing, and why?
4. What is the difference between treating the gospel as a proposition and receiving it as God's power?
5. In what ways are you still 'growing into' the gospel?

## Application
- (video) The gospel is not an idea, but God's saving action in relationship: His covenant faithfulness extended to all who believe in Jesus Christ and respond with lives marked by faithfulness to Him. The teacher confesses that as a young believer he treated the gospel as a proposition to defend with arguments. A mentor's words changed that: 'We never outgrow the gospel. We simply grow more and more into the gospel.' God was under no obligation to choose any of us (1 Peter 2:9); what we deserved was wrath, and what He gave was the power of His salvation.
- Study note (added): this week, read Romans 1:16-17 each morning and name one place where you are tempted to be quiet about Jesus; ask God for courage there.
